---
title: "Why ordinary beta regression does not fit endpoint sliders"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The beta density has support $0<y<1$. MegaNegRaising contains exact zeros and ones on both recorded sliders, so ordinary beta regression assigns those observations zero probability.

```{r}
#| label: load-meganegraising-beta
#| echo: true
mnr <- read.csv("data/meganegraising/meganegraising-balanced.csv")
endpoint_counts <- data.frame(
  response = rep(c("neg-raising", "ease"), each = 3L),
  region = rep(c("zero", "interior", "one"), times = 2L),
  observations = c(sum(mnr$negraising == 0),
                   sum(mnr$negraising > 0 & mnr$negraising < 1),
                   sum(mnr$negraising == 1),
                   sum(mnr$acceptability == 0),
                   sum(mnr$acceptability > 0 & mnr$acceptability < 1),
                   sum(mnr$acceptability == 1))
)
endpoint_counts
```

For $0<y<1$, a mean–precision beta parameterization is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\mu_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi}.
$$

Neither density value at an endpoint is a probability mass. A common workaround nudges every observation with

$$
y_i^*=\frac{y_i(n-1)+1/2}{n}.
$$

The consequence is data-dependent and should be computed, not illustrated with chosen values.

```{r}
#| label: actual-endpoint-nudge
#| echo: true
n <- nrow(mnr)
transform_endpoint <- function(y) (y * (n - 1) + .5) / n
data.frame(recorded = c(0, 1), transformed = transform_endpoint(c(0, 1)),
           sample_size = n)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-endpoint-nudge
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
plot_data <- transform(endpoint_counts,
                       probability = observations / ave(observations, response, FUN = sum))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(region, probability, shape = response, group = response)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .25), size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Observed region", y = "Proportion", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

For the `r n` retained judgments, zero becomes `r format(transform_endpoint(0), digits = 6)` and one becomes `r format(transform_endpoint(1), digits = 6)`. The transformation makes the sample size part of the measurement model: adding unrelated rows moves the transformed endpoints. It also replaces observed endpoint events with extremely interior values.

A likelihood that contains explicit endpoint probabilities is more faithful to the recorded response. The next page uses ordered-beta regression for both sliders without changing or filtering either outcome.
